288.title: The small holocaust, 1746
288.hook: thousands of Sikhs are killed in a campaign near Kahnuwan
288.tomorrow: The Dal Khalsa and the council
288.howItsDone: Sikhs remember the Chhota Ghallughara of 1746 in their histories and at gurdwaras, and the martyrs of the eighteenth century are named in general terms in Ardas, the daily prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kesh: he kept his kesh. Today is a day of remembering, and it asks for a gentle pace.

Some families have a year nobody mentions lightly. The year of the flood, the fire, the war. The older relatives lower their voices when it comes up, and the children learn, without being told, that this is something you remember carefully. The Sikh community has two years like that in the eighteenth century, and they have names. The first came in 1746, in the marshes and hills of northern Punjab. Today: Chhota Ghallughara, the small holocaust.
screen: `A YEAR FAMILIES REMEMBER CAREFULLY.` → `TWO SUCH YEARS, WITH NAMES.` → `THE FIRST: 1746.`

segments.voice: Ghallughara is the Punjabi word Sikhs use for a massacre, a great destruction. Chhota means small, only because a larger one would come sixteen years later. In 1746 Lakhpat Rai, a senior official in Lahore, lost his brother in a clash with a Sikh band, and swore to wipe out the Sikhs in return. First, Sikhs living in Lahore were rounded up and killed. Then he led a large army, with cannon, to the marshy forest of Kahnuwan, near the Beas and Ravi rivers. Thousands of Sikhs were camped there: fighters, along with women, children and old people. They fled north toward the hills, hoping for shelter, and were trapped between the soldiers behind them, a swollen river, and hill rulers who wouldn't let them in. Over several weeks in the early summer, thousands were killed, and many who were captured were taken to Lahore and executed. The numbers in the old accounts vary, often around seven thousand killed and three thousand captured. Nobody knows exactly. Sikhs don't tell this story to stir up hatred. The people who did this are long gone, and no one living today carries the blame. They tell it so the people who died aren't forgotten, and because of what came next. The survivors regrouped. Within a few years they were stronger and better organized than before. That's tomorrow's story.

segments.voice: A minute of silence: sit still, hands resting, with nothing to imagine and nothing in particular to feel. Just hold a quiet space for people you'll never know, who were lost that summer, and for anyone, anywhere, whose family carries a year like that. If you pray, let the silence be your prayer.
Chhota Ghallughara. The small holocaust of 1746, when thousands of Sikhs were killed in a campaign near Kahnuwan. Remembered, not turned to hate.
Your line: remembered. A quiet day, and an important one. See you tomorrow.

289.title: The Dal Khalsa and the council
289.hook: Sikh bands unite, meeting at Amritsar and deciding together before the Guru
289.howItsDone: Sikh assemblies still pass gurmatas, resolutions made in the presence of the Guru Granth Sahib and sealed with Ardas; the Sarbat Khalsa, a gathering of the whole community at the Akal Takht, is the traditional forum.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Chhota Ghallughara: remembered. The survivors grew stronger. Today, how: they learned to decide together.

A simple plan can take three days in a group chat. Everyone has an opinion, two people aren't speaking, and in the end nothing happens. Now make the group many independent bands of riders, each with its own leader, its own pride, its own old quarrels. And the stakes aren't dinner plans. They're survival. The Sikhs of the 1740s found a way to make that group decide, and stick to it. It happened twice a year, in Amritsar. Today: gurmata.
screen: `THE GROUP CHAT THAT NEVER DECIDES.` → `MANY PROUD BANDS.` → `TWICE A YEAR, IN AMRITSAR.`

segments.voice: Gurmata joins two words: gur, the Guru, and mata, a resolution, a considered decision. A gurmata is a decision made in the presence of the Guru, and so binding on everyone. Even in the hunted years, the scattered Sikh bands tried to gather at Amritsar at Vaisakhi in spring and Diwali in autumn. The whole assembly was called the Sarbat Khalsa, the entire Khalsa. They met before the Akal Takht, with the Guru Granth Sahib present. Leaders who might be rivals the rest of the year sat down together, and old quarrels were supposed to be left at the door. Matters were discussed openly, and when the assembly agreed, it was sealed with Ardas, the prayer. From then on it was a gurmata: not one leader's plan but the Guru's decision, and every band was bound by it. A turning point came at Vaisakhi, 1748, two years after the small holocaust. The Sarbat Khalsa resolved to bring the many bands together into one army, the Dal Khalsa, the army of the Khalsa, under a single commander, Jassa Singh Ahluwalia. Separate bands, one body. What gave the decision its weight wasn't the loudest voice or the biggest band. It was the presence of the Guru, and the agreement of the whole. The Sikh Rehat Maryada, the Sikh code of conduct, still describes how a gurmata is made. There's a small lesson in it for any family or team. A decision made together, in front of what everyone respects, holds better than one forced through. And the thing everyone bows to can be bigger than anyone in the room.

segments.voice: Think of a decision coming up that affects other people: what to cook, where to go, how to split a job, a family plan. Notice whether you meant to decide it yourself, or let it drift. Then picture asking the others, listening properly, and choosing together, with something you all care about in the middle of the table.

290.title: Baba Deep Singh, 1757
290.hook: the old scholar-warrior rides to free the Harmandir; tradition says he fought on with his head in his hand
290.howItsDone: Pilgrims at the Harmandir Sahib stop at the place in the parikrama where tradition says Baba Deep Singh fell, and Gurdwara Shaheedan in Amritsar honors him and his companions; his birthday and martyrdom are marked each year.

segments.voice: Yesterday, gurmata: decide together. Today, a promise made by one old man, and kept.

Walk around the pool at the Golden Temple and you'll pass a small shrine where people stop, bow and whisper. Many visitors are surprised by the painting they often see of the man it remembers: an old warrior with a long white beard, sword in one hand, his own head held in the other. It sounds like a legend. Sikhs tell it with love and awe, and they'll also tell you why it matters more than the miracle. Today: Baba Deep Singh.
screen: `A SMALL SHRINE BY THE POOL.` → `SWORD IN ONE HAND.` → `HIS HEAD IN THE OTHER.`

segments.voice: Baba means elder, grandfather, a title of love for someone old and wise. Deep Singh was, first of all, a scholar. Tradition says he took amrit from Guru Gobind Singh himself, and spent years at Damdama Sahib, the Guru's seat of learning, copying the Guru Granth Sahib by hand so more Sikhs could have it. Some of those copies were sent to the takhts. He was also a warrior, and by 1757 an old one, around seventy-five. That year, forces of the Afghan king Ahmad Shah Abdali occupied Amritsar and desecrated the Harmandir. When the news reached Damdama Sahib, Baba Deep Singh made a vow: he would go to Amritsar and free it, or die trying. Riders joined him along the way. Tradition says he drew a line on the ground and asked only those ready to give their lives to cross it. The Afghan army met them a few miles from Amritsar, and the fighting was fierce. Here the accounts differ. The best-known tradition says his head was struck off, and he held it on his palm and fought on until he reached the sacred precinct, and laid it there. Other accounts say he was mortally wounded in the neck and fought on to the end. Either way, he finished what he'd vowed. Sikhs find the image powerful because it pictures a promise that outlasts even the body. Most of us make small vows every week, and leave them half done. Baba Deep Singh is the old man who finished his.

291.title: The great holocaust, 1762
291.hook: Ahmad Shah Abdali's army kills a great many Sikhs in a day, then blows up the Harmandir
291.howItsDone: Sikhs remember the Vadda Ghallughara each year, especially near Kup-Rahira, where a memorial and gurdwara stand; the rebuilding of the Harmandir after 1764 is remembered as the panth rising again.

segments.voice: Yesterday, baba: finish the vow. Today is the second of those two years Sikhs remember carefully.

A winter morning in February, 1762, on the flat farmland southwest of Ludhiana. A long, slow column moves across the fields. Not an army, mostly. Families. Grandparents on carts, children on their mothers' hips, cooking pots, cattle, everything they own, heading for safety in the dry country to the south. The fighters ride alongside. And then, on the horizon, dust. An army that had marched through the night. Today: Vadda Ghallughara, the great holocaust.
screen: `FEBRUARY, 1762.` → `A COLUMN OF FAMILIES.` → `DUST ON THE HORIZON.`

segments.voice: Vadda means great, large. Ghallughara, as you heard a few days ago, means a massacre, a great destruction. The army belonged to Ahmad Shah Abdali, the king of Afghanistan, who invaded northern India many times. He had marched fast to catch the Sikhs off guard, near the village of Kup. The Sikh fighters did something remarkable. They formed a moving ring around the families and kept the whole column walking, fighting on the outside while the old and the young moved in the middle, all through the day. But the losses were terrible. Many thousands were killed in that one day, among them many women, children and old people. The old accounts give numbers from about ten thousand to far more. Nobody knows exactly. That spring, at Vaisakhi, Abdali came to Amritsar. His men packed the Harmandir with gunpowder and blew it up, and filled the sacred pool with rubble. It looked like the end. It wasn't. That same autumn, the Sikhs gathered at Amritsar at Diwali and faced Abdali's army again, and he withdrew. Within two years they were rebuilding the Harmandir and clearing the pool, brick by brick. Soon after, the Sikhs held Lahore. So the Sikh memory of 1762 has two halves. One is grief, held carefully and without hatred for anyone living today. The other is the comeback, told with quiet pride: the panth rose again.

Your line: the panth rose again. Grief and comeback, both remembered. Rest well, and see you tomorrow.

292.title: The Misls
292.hook: twelve Sikh confederacies rule parts of Punjab in the late 1700s
292.howItsDone: Some Sikh families still trace their history to one of the twelve misls; the misl period is taught in Sikh history as the bridge between the persecution of the early 1700s and the kingdom of Maharaja Ranjit Singh.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Vadda Ghallughara: the panth rose again. Today, what the panth rose into.

A big extended family can work like a small federation. Every household runs its own home, its own budget, its own arguments. Cousins compete. Uncles don't always speak. But for a wedding, a funeral, or someone in trouble, everyone shows up, and for a day they're one family. In the late 1700s, Punjab was run a little like that. After decades of being hunted, the Sikhs now held the land, not as one kingdom, but as twelve. Today: the misls.
screen: `MANY HOUSEHOLDS, ONE FAMILY.` → `EVERYONE SHOWS UP.` → `PUNJAB IN THE 1700S: TWELVE.`

segments.voice: A misl was a Sikh confederacy: a band of fighters and their families under a leader, a sardar, holding its own territory. By the second half of the 1700s, as Afghan and Mughal power in Punjab faded, there were twelve main misls. Some took their names from a leader's village, some from a trait. The Bhangis, who at one time held Lahore and Amritsar. The Ahluwalias, led by Jassa Singh, the commander of the Dal Khalsa. The Ramgarhias, the Kanhaiyas, the Sukerchakias, and others. Each ran its own affairs, and they did not always get along. Misls competed, feuded, and sometimes fought each other; historians don't hide that. Sources differ on where the word comes from. It's Arabic. Some explain it as alike or equal, because the misls were meant to be equals; others as a file or record, because the bands were listed in one register. Both fit. Here's what makes the misls more than a set of rival chiefdoms. Twice a year, at Vaisakhi and Diwali, they still came to Amritsar as the Sarbat Khalsa, sat before the Guru Granth Sahib, and could pass a gurmata together. Faced with an outside threat, the twelve could move as one Dal Khalsa. Many also offered rakhi, protection, to villages in return for a share of the harvest. It was untidy, and it lasted only a few decades. But it held the Sikhs together through a dangerous time, and one of those twelve would soon produce a young leader who'd unite most of them.

293.title: Maharaja Ranjit Singh
293.hook: he unites Punjab in 1799 and covers the Harmandir in gold, giving it the name the world knows
293.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Maharaja Ranjit Singh as the ruler of the Sikh Empire; his samadhi stands in Lahore, and the gilding he gave to Harmandir Sahib, which Sikhs often call Darbar Sahib, is renewed and cared for to this day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the misls: twelve, and one. Today, the young leader from one of those twelve who made them one kingdom.

A shining building sits in the middle of a still pool, its upper walls and dome glowing gold, reflected upside down in the water. Pilgrims walk around it barefoot, day and night. Photos of it hang on kitchen walls and glow on phone screens around the world. But it didn't always look like that. For generations it stood in brick and stone. The gold came later, from a king. Today: Maharaja Ranjit Singh.
screen: `A SHINING BUILDING IN A STILL POOL.` → `ON WALLS AND PHONES WORLDWIDE.` → `THE GOLD CAME LATER.`

segments.voice: Ranjit Singh was born in 1780, the son of the leader of the Sukerchakia misl. As a small child he survived smallpox, which left him blind in one eye. He became chief as a boy, and in 1799, still a young man, he rode into Lahore and took the city. Over the next years he brought the misls and much of the land around them under one rule, and in 1801 he was proclaimed Maharaja, great king, of Punjab. He ruled for almost forty years, until his death in 1839. His was a Sikh kingdom, but not only for Sikhs. Muslims and Hindus served at the top of his government; his foreign minister was a Muslim scholar. Then there's the gold. Ranjit Singh gave generously to many places of worship, and above all to the Harmandir in Amritsar, the temple the Afghans had destroyed and the Sikhs had rebuilt. Over years of work, its upper stories were covered in gilded copper, with inlaid marble added below. English-speaking visitors called it the Golden Temple, and the name stuck. Sikhs usually call it Harmandir Sahib, the house of God, or Darbar Sahib, the Guru's court. Sikhs love to tell one story about him. Accused once of breaking the Sikh code, the Maharaja was summoned before the Akal Takht, and he went, bowed, and accepted its judgment like any other Sikh. Remember the two flags at the Akal Takht, the flag of the spirit standing a little higher? That day, the king took his place beneath it.

294.title: Annexation, 1849
294.hook: after two wars with the British, Punjab is annexed and the boy king Duleep Singh sent to England
294.howItsDone: Sikhs remember the annexation of 1849 as the end of the Sikh kingdom; Maharaja Duleep Singh's story is widely told in the Sikh diaspora, especially in Britain, where a statue of him stands in Thetford, Norfolk.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Maharaja: the golden temple. Today, what happened to his kingdom and his youngest son, then a look back at the week.

A ten-year-old boy sits on a throne too big for him. He's the king, officially. His mother has been taken from him. Grown men decide his future over his head. One spring day in 1849, he's asked to sign a paper that gives away his kingdom, and a diamond famous across the world. A few years later, he'll be living in England, thousands of miles from Punjab. Today: annexation, and the boy king Duleep Singh.
screen: `A TEN-YEAR-OLD ON A THRONE.` → `A PAPER TO SIGN, 1849.` → `THOUSANDS OF MILES FROM PUNJAB.`

segments.voice: After Ranjit Singh died in 1839, his kingdom fell into a decade of turmoil: rulers came and went, and several were killed. The British East India Company, already ruling much of India, was watching. Two wars with the British followed, in 1845 and 1848. The Sikh armies fought hard, and some battles cost the British dearly. But the kingdom lost. In March 1849, Punjab was annexed, taken into British India. The last Maharaja, Duleep Singh, Ranjit Singh's youngest son, was about ten. He was separated from his mother, Maharani Jind Kaur, and placed with a British guardian, and the Koh-i-Noor diamond was sent to Queen Victoria. As a young teenager he became a Christian, and at fifteen he was taken to England, where he lived as a country gentleman. As a young man he was allowed to bring his mother to England, and she lived near him until her death. Years later, in his forties, he tried to return to Punjab and took up his Sikh faith once more. He was stopped on the way, and died in Paris in 1893, far from home. Sikhs remember him with a particular ache: the king who lost his home, his mother and his kingdom as a child. Now the week. The Chhota Ghallughara: remembered. Gurmata: decide together. Baba Deep Singh: finish the vow. The Vadda Ghallughara: the panth rose again. The misls: twelve, and one. Ranjit Singh: the golden temple. And annexation: far from home.
